answer.label: Not Napoleon Bonaparte — actually Robert J. Hanlon
answer.authorDates: fl. 1980 · American computer programmer, Tobyhanna Army Depot
answer.sourceLine: This is “Hanlon’s Razor.” Quote Investigator traces its earliest documented appearance to the 1980 humor anthology Murphy’s Law Book Two, where it is credited to Robert J. Hanlon — there worded “Never attribute to malice….” The “ascribe” wording is a later variant, and QI found no substantive support for the popular Napoleon Bonaparte attribution.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: “ascribe” is a later variant of the 1980 “attribute”

source.excerpt: Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.
trail: Quote Investigator finds the earliest close match in the 1980 anthology Murphy’s Law Book Two, edited by Arthur Bloch, where it is printed as “Hanlon’s Razor” and credited to Robert J. Hanlon.
Per QI, Hanlon was a computer programmer who submitted the line for inclusion after reading Bloch’s original Murphy’s Law; QI concludes he “should be credited with the saying.”
QI states it “has found no substantive support for ascribing the statement to Napoleon Bonaparte,” and Wikipedia likewise notes a similar quote is “misattributed to Napoleon.”

Thematic ancestors exist — Robert Heinlein’s 1941 Logic of Empire (“You have attributed conditions to villainy that simply result from stupidity”) — but none is the exact modern razor, which QI dates to Hanlon.
source.excerptNote: The wording as first published in 1980. The version circulated under Napoleon’s name swaps “attribute” for “ascribe.”

source.rightsNote: The saying’s earliest documented publication is the 1980 anthology Murphy’s Law Book Two, well after 1931, so the specific coined text is in copyright in the United States. There is no pre-1931 source to make it public domain, and the Napoleon attribution rests on no traceable work at all.

author.name: Robert J. Hanlon
author.heading: About Robert J. Hanlon
author.metaLine: fl. 1980 · American computer programmer, Tobyhanna Army Depot, Pennsylvania
author.bio: Robert J. Hanlon was a computer programmer at the Tobyhanna Army Depot near Scranton, Pennsylvania. According to Quote Investigator, he submitted his aphorism for inclusion in a sequel to Arthur Bloch’s Murphy’s Law, and it was printed in the 1980 collection Murphy’s Law Book Two as “Hanlon’s Razor.” The name was coined by analogy to Occam’s Razor, and the line has since been widely — and wrongly — reassigned to grander names, Napoleon chief among them.

misattribution.heading: How this landed on Napoleon
misattribution.intro: A crisp, cynical one-liner about human folly is exactly the kind of quote that drifts toward a famous strategist. But the paper trail runs to a 1980 joke book, not to any Napoleonic letter or memoir.

items.why: Quote Investigator states it “has found no substantive support for ascribing the statement to Napoleon Bonaparte” (QI). The “ascribe”-worded Napoleon version surfaces in aggregators traced only to a 2003 book, with no primary Napoleonic source.

Heinlein’s 1941 novella Logic of Empire has a character say “you have attributed conditions to villainy that simply result from stupidity” (Wikipedia) — the same idea, but not the razor’s exact wording.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is Hanlon’s Razor, first documented in the 1980 anthology Murphy’s Law Book Two and credited to Robert J. Hanlon — not Napoleon (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line endures because it is a genuinely useful rule of thumb: in a world of cock-ups and confusion, incompetence explains far more than conspiracy. Coined in a lighthearted anthology of “laws” alongside Murphy’s, it graduated into serious use in engineering, management, and internet culture as “Hanlon’s Razor.”

Its attachment to Napoleon is a textbook case of quote-drift: an anonymous-sounding maxim gains gravity when pinned to a famous commander known for hard-nosed judgments about people. The upgrade is flattering but unsupported.
context.pull: Incompetence explains more than conspiracy — but Hanlon, not Napoleon, said so.
